desc:
Find the shortest contiguous substring (window) of s that contains t as a subsequence, that is, all characters of t appear inside the window in the same order, though not necessarily next to each other. Return the length of that window, or 0 if no window works.

For example, for s = "abcdebdde" and t = "bde" the answer is 4 (the window "bcde"). For s = "axbxc" and t = "abc" the answer is 5, and for s = "abc" and t = "ca" it is 0.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase letters and digits
hints: Checking every substring of s for the subsequence property is far too slow. First think about the cheaper question: for a fixed end position, where is the best place to start?
For each prefix of t of length j, track the largest start index such that t[0..j) is a subsequence of the window starting there and ending at the current position of s.

When you read s[i] and it equals t[j-1], the best start for prefix j becomes the best start for prefix j-1 (as it was before this character). Process j in decreasing order so a character is not used twice. Whenever the full t has a start, i - start + 1 is a candidate window.
editorial: Let start[j] be the maximum index p such that t[0..j) is a subsequence of s[p..i], or -1 if none exists. Reading the next character s[i], for every j with t[j-1] == s[i] we can finish prefix j here, using the best start of prefix j-1 from before: start[j] = start[j-1] (for j = 1 the start is simply i). Updating j from high to low prevents the same character of s from matching two positions of t.

Each time start[m] (m = len(t)) is set, the window [start[m], i] is a candidate and the shortest candidate is the answer. Keeping the latest start is right because a later start only shortens the window. The cost is O(|s| · |t|) in the worst case; indexing, for every character, the positions in t where it occurs lets the loop skip non-matching j. A naive search that tries all starts and greedily matches is O(|s|²) and too slow at 10,000.
